Architecture 2.0 asks whether learned models, coupled directly to physical engineering tools and closed-loop feedback, can let an architecture study revisit more of a design's hardware–software interfaces, memory hierarchy, and execution schedule than a manual flow allows. The moonshot is a design system capable of carrying high-level system intent through to a verified, physically realizable chip. Throughout that process, human architects set the requirements, examine the measured evidence, and remain responsible for the final commitment to silicon.

Historical precedents from Mead–Conway VLSI, RISC, and logic synthesis show that new design abstractions take hold only when paired with dependable implementation and verification tools. Building on those lessons, this chapter separates point assistance and parameter tuning from full AI-native workflows according to which hardware and software decisions each workflow can revisit. A concrete edge-device challenge then grounds the discussion, showing how a compact product request expands into measurable constraints, execution traces, and checkable silicon contracts (@fig-ch01-cover-map).

Judging whether a design system meets those contracts requires separating two questions: how good the resulting chip is, and how much engineering effort it took to develop and verify. That distinction lets architects compare new automated demonstrations against strong conventional baselines while the full moonshot capability remains an active research frontier.

![**From a system goal to evaluated candidate designs.** A high-level system request expands into explicit constraints and workload specifications, followed by coordinated design experiments using learned models and engineering tools. Evaluation separates design quality from the engineering effort needed to develop and verify candidates, providing evidence for human review rather than authorizing autonomous tapeout decisions.](images/ch01-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch01-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Chapter overview diagram in which a system goal leads to explicit requirements, coordinated design experiments, and evaluation of the design and the effort needed to develop it, followed by human review."}

## Why Manual Design Loops No Longer Keep Up {#sec-case-for-ai-native-design}

Consider an architect tasked with accelerating a target workload under fixed power and chip-area constraints. Increasing on-chip memory capacity can reduce stall cycles, but consumes precious die area and leakage power. Reorganizing the computation might extract more throughput from existing hardware, but demands extensive software rewrites. The architect's challenge is to determine which combination of microarchitectural and software choices satisfies the constraints, and whether the gains justify the design cost.

These trade-offs have grown sharply more consequential as frequency and energy-efficiency gains from classic transistor scaling have stalled, forcing system gains to rely on parallelism, domain specialization, and aggressive hardware–software co-design [@HennessyPatterson2019GoldenAge]. Yet a specialized accelerator multiplies the architectural degrees of freedom across work partitioning, on-chip buffer sizes, interconnect bandwidth, and memory consistency. Because every workload shift can reopen these decisions while implementing, simulating, and verifying candidates consumes the exploration budget, the compounding scaling pressures developed in @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales force a fundamental operational question: how can architecture teams explore a wide enough space of alternatives, with sufficient physical fidelity, within practical project budgets?

Machine learning offers methods to navigate this search, not as an autonomous, monolithic replacement for the architect, but as a suite of predictive, generative, and optimization techniques.[^fn-historical-ai-c01] Learned cost models can rank tensor-program schedules before running them on hardware [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]; generative models can draft initial register-transfer logic [@VerilogEval]. The deeper opportunity, however, lies in integrating these techniques into a closed loop with physical tools, so that simulation and timing feedback guide the next round of proposals. That integration makes the organization of the design process itself a central architectural question.

[^fn-historical-ai-c01]: **Historical AI in Architecture**: Learning has a history both in hardware mechanisms, such as perceptron branch predictors [@JimenezLin2001Perceptron], and in design tools, such as predictive models for design-space exploration [@IpekEtAl2006PredictiveDSE]. This chapter concerns the design process, where learned components can help propose and assess changes to the hardware and software under study.

These learned components bring a second engineering obligation into the design process. For a conventional memory controller, engineers specify the required behavior, implement the control logic, and verify conformance to that specification. For a learned cost predictor, engineers choose the training examples and objective, fit the model, and assess its predictions on independent examples to determine how well it generalizes [@HastieTibshiraniFriedman2009Elements]. The familiar sequence of specify, implement, and verify therefore meets a complementary discipline of learn and validate. Both remain necessary. A conventional implementation must still serve its intended purpose, while a learned component still has interfaces and explicit requirements that can be checked.

In Architecture 2.0, learning can reside in the design process even when the resulting hardware is conventional. A model may propose a memory controller whose functional behavior and timing still require verification. Whether the complete design process finds useful controllers across workloads and resource limits is a separate empirical question. That assessment requires problems withheld from development of the process, credible alternative methods, and accounting for the cost of unsuccessful attempts. One verified controller supports a claim about that candidate; validating the process requires evidence across the conditions in which architects intend to use it.

For each proposed memory subsystem, a generated controller or software schedule is only an initial hypothesis. Cycle-level simulators must measure its performance, synthesis and layout tools must check its timing and area, thermal models must test whether its power dissipation fits the package and cooling limits, and functional checks must confirm that it matches the specification. If a candidate delivers high throughput but misses timing, that result should guide the next experiment, prompting the system to pipeline critical paths, adjust tile sizes, or drop the branch. Progress comes from repeating this loop: proposing an architectural change, measuring its physical cost, and using the result to steer the search.

This closed loop defines the Architecture 2.0 moonshot: coordinating cross-layer exploration from high-level system intent down to a physically realizable design. An automated system formalizes architecture questions, bounds the search space, and couples learned proposals directly to physical electronic design automation (EDA) tools, making it practical to evaluate alternatives that manual flows never have time to consider. The capability remains a demanding research frontier. Its value will not be proved by fast isolated demos or synthetic code-generation benchmarks, but by finding better architectural trade-offs, cutting total engineering effort, or both, when measured against strong conventional baselines.

## Lessons from Earlier Shifts in Design Automation {#sec-historical-context}

Major transitions in computer architecture history offer clear precedents for this shift. Each breakthrough redefined how architects express design intent and evaluate trade-offs, and each succeeded only because it was anchored by dependable implementation tools and rigorous checking infrastructure. These milestones show what any new automated workflow must provide before engineers can trust its results.

The Mead–Conway very-large-scale integration (VLSI) revolution decoupled topological circuit layout from foundry-specific fabrication recipes through scalable, dimensionless $\lambda$-rules [@MeadConway1980VLSI].[^fn-vlsi-complexity-c01] Designers could compose complex layouts using a uniform geometric contract without managing individual process physics. This division of responsibility proved essential as transistor budgets expanded: architects could focus on modular system composition while design rules supplied a checkable connection to the fabrication process.

[^fn-vlsi-complexity-c01]: **VLSI complexity (origin)**: Early-1980s frontier microprocessors held about $10^4$ to $10^5$ transistors, and by 2021 frontier chips held tens of billions [@Rupp2022MicroprocessorTrendData]. Mead and Conway answered that outgrowth of transistor-level practice with higher-level abstractions, design rules, and fabrication access that a course could teach and a community could share.

While Mead–Conway separated layout geometry from process physics, reduced-instruction-set computing (RISC) showed that other boundaries must be evaluated together: an instruction-set architecture cannot be judged apart from compiler behavior and physical cycle time [@PattersonDitzel1980RISC]. An instruction's value depends on whether optimizing compilers actually use it and how much pipeline complexity it adds to the hardware. That insight made the compiler a full partner in architectural design, judging an instruction set by end-to-end program runtime and clock rate rather than by the compactness of hand-written assembly code.

On the hardware implementation side, logic synthesis raised the level at which engineers describe circuits. Once architects specified computation as register-transfer level (RTL) operations on data and state, synthesis tools could translate those descriptions directly into optimized gate netlists [@DeMicheli1994SynthesisOptimization]. Synthesis earned engineering trust, however, only because it was paired with two verification pillars that made its output auditable: formal equivalence checking proved functional agreement between RTL and gates [@Formality], while static timing analysis (STA) checked path delays against declared clock and timing constraints without requiring exhaustive dynamic simulation.[^fn-formal-sta-c01] Generating a gate-level circuit and proving its functional and timing validity became inseparable halves of the design flow.

[^fn-formal-sta-c01]: **Equivalence checking and timing analysis**: Formal equivalence checking proves that two circuit representations (such as register-transfer level source and a synthesized gate netlist) agree under the proof's state and input assumptions without enumerating simulation test vectors. Static timing analysis (STA) checks setup and hold constraints using path delays and declared clock relationships at specified operating corners. Asynchronous clock-domain crossings require separate checks for synchronization and protocol safety.

Parameterized hardware generators extended this foundation by encoding entire families of microarchitectures as software programs. Hardware construction languages such as Chisel parameterize datapath bitwidths, cache capacities, and buffer depths, allowing generators to emit customized RTL descriptions across broad design spaces [@BachrachEtAl2012Chisel].[^fn-generators-c01] Yet parameterization alone does not resolve the design problem: architects must still evaluate the generated instances. A generator can encode alternative topologies or pipeline structures, but its existing parameters cannot express a repair outside the family it was written to construct.

[^fn-generators-c01]: **Hardware generators**: Unlike static register-transfer descriptions, hardware generators are programs written in host languages (such as Scala in Chisel) that emit a register-transfer description during an elaboration phase (Chisel produces an intermediate representation, FIRRTL, that is lowered to Verilog). Their parameters can select both dimensions and structural alternatives. Exploring beyond those alternatives requires revising the generator or supplying a different construction method.

Across each of these transitions, an abstraction made larger design problems tractable only when paired with dependable implementation tools and automated verification checks (@fig-design-method-progression).
