The proposed design system would extend this relationship to coordinated hardware–software exploration. Its separate placement marks it as a research ambition.](images/fig-design-method-progression){#fig-design-method-progression width="100%" fig-pos="!htbp" fig-alt="Diagram in which four historical examples arranged in two rows connect VLSI design rules, instruction-set choices, RTL, and parameterized generators to implementations and their checks. A separate proposed system connects a system goal and current design files to methods, tools, and evaluated alternatives."}

Architecture 2.0 proposes the next logical step in this progression. Just as Mead–Conway decoupled layout from process chemistry, and logic synthesis decoupled RTL behavior from gate-level boolean logic, Architecture 2.0 seeks to decouple compact architectural intent from the manual coordination of cross-stack tools and representations. The input is a high-level system specification, and the design loop coordinates candidate generation, simulation, and physical implementation across layers. As in every previous transition, raising the level of abstraction works only when backed by explicit verification and signoff checks that engineers can audit.

## Three Scopes of AI-Assisted Architecture {#sec-three-operational-layers}

When an engineering team lumps all "AI for chip design" together, expectations quickly outrun what a given tool can actually change. A local Verilog autocomplete model cannot relieve a system-wide memory bottleneck, and a parameter tuner cannot close a power gap if the frozen bus interface itself prevents every legal configuration from meeting the budget. Drafting an isolated cache controller, sweeping its capacities inside a fixed bus protocol, and redesigning the memory hierarchy alongside its compiler runtime require very different levels of coordination across the system stack.

That coordination matters because computer architecture spans both the hardware–software contract and the physical structures that implement it: instruction set architecture (ISA), microarchitecture, memory hierarchy, interconnect fabrics, specialized accelerators, chiplet topologies, compiler schedules, and runtime interfaces. Because these layers depend on one another (a wider vector datapath helps only if compiler vectorization, memory bandwidth, and thermal limits can feed and cool it), changing one layer in isolation often exposes a bottleneck in another.

To distinguish how much of this stack a workflow can adjust, Architecture 2.0 defines three operational layers [@ReddiYazdanbakhsh2025Architecture20]. Rather than categorizing tools by the algorithms they run, the layers classify a workflow by which design decisions it may revisit. Architects still set the constraints, weigh cross-layer trade-offs, and make the final signoff decisions, while an AI-native system makes more of the search between those checkpoints executable in a closed loop, especially when fixing a bottleneck requires changing hardware and software together.

### Scope of the Design Loop

Suppose a memory subsystem stalls because continuous sensor traffic saturates the processor–cache bus. Whether an automated workflow can relieve that stall depends on which parts of the design the human team has frozen in advance and which parts the tool is allowed to change. Across the three operational layers, workflows differ in what inputs the architect supplies, which design choices remain open to search, and what output the system returns (@tbl-operational-layers-input-output). Because the classification depends on this design scope rather than on the underlying algorithm, an engineer who prompts a foundation model and one who runs a numerical optimizer may be working in the same layer. Moving from Layer 1 to Layer 3, the human team fixes less of the hardware and software structure up front, and the automated loop can revise more of it (@fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration).

- **Layer 1 (point assistance): Assistance with Individual Tasks within a Frozen Context.** The input is an isolated request (such as drafting an RTL block, writing a unit testbench, or diagnosing a static timing report) inside an existing, human-designed architecture whose system organization, microarchitecture, bus interfaces, and tool flow remain fixed. Because the system can vary only the local code, logic, or estimate needed for that single task, it returns a standalone candidate artifact; the human engineer then reviews the output, fixes errors, integrates the block, and decides what to run next. In our memory subsystem study, for example, an architect might ask a code-generation model to draft an AXI4-Stream first-in, first-out (FIFO) queue or a parameterizable cache controller module, after which the engineer inspects the generated Verilog, wires its ports into the existing system-on-chip (SoC) crossbar, chooses the cache capacity, and runs lint and timing checks. Point assistance speeds up one local step while the surrounding architectural study stays manual.
- **Layer 2 (container-bound optimization): Parameter Optimization within an Immutable Formulation.** The inputs are (1) the target workload, (2) the physical power, performance, and area (PPA) constraints, and (3) a parameterized architectural design space $\Theta$ bounded by fixed interfaces. Before search begins, human architects define the parameterized template (such as allowable cache capacities, buffer depths, array aspect ratios, pipeline stage counts, compiler unroll flags, or circuit macro coordinates), keeping the template, its legal parameter ranges, and its external interfaces fixed even when parameters select among different internal topologies. The search varies only the parameter vector $\theta \in \Theta$, evaluating candidates in a closed loop with simulators or electronic design automation (EDA) tools to return the best configuration $\theta^*$ (or an estimated Pareto frontier) inside that space. In our memory study, an optimizer tunes the memory hierarchy by searching cache line sizes, capacities, and set associativities against cycle-accurate simulation while holding the processor-cache bus interface, coherence protocol, and workload binary fixed. If none of those parameter settings can relieve a DRAM bandwidth bottleneck, the optimizer cannot escape the bottleneck by changing the memory interface or rewriting the software. Learned macro placement, which searches $(x,y)$ coordinates for circuit blocks within a fixed netlist, follows this same pattern [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement].
- **Layer 3 (AI-native design system): Specification-Driven Co-Design across Abstraction Boundaries.** The inputs are (1) the workload requirements (such as a computational graph, kernel specification, or execution trace), (2) the physical PPA targets and process limits (power budget, clock period, silicon area, thermal dissipation, and process design kit), and (3) a correctness and verification contract (a functional golden model or formal specification). Rather than staying inside a single microarchitectural template, the system can make coordinated changes across the layers the team has opened to search: proposing new microarchitectural organizations, changing arithmetic formats (such as replacing two's complement ripple addition with carry-save redundant forms), revising dataflow schedules (such as switching from output-stationary to weight-stationary execution with on-chip double buffering), adding custom instruction extensions, and adapting compiler lowering passes to match. Physical feedback from downstream tools guides upstream architectural changes, returning a co-adapted hardware–software candidate together with its measured metrics and any unmet constraints, while human architects set the requirements, audit the verification contracts, and judge the final trade-offs. Although the moonshot aims for a complete design that passes physical signoff, a given run may reject its candidates or halt with unresolved violations, and the public end-to-end demonstrations reviewed in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect carry specifications toward layout without yet beating a matched conventional baseline once total engineering cost is counted. In our memory study, instead of tuning a standard cache hierarchy, a Layer 3 system could inspect memory stall traces and recognize that hardware cache tags waste area and power on streaming accesses. It could then replace the cache with an explicit scratchpad, software-managed direct memory access (DMA) descriptor queues, double-buffered streaming FIFOs, and matching compiler loop schedules that overlap compute with data transfers, before checking the combined design against timing and power signoff.

| **Operational layer** | **Inputs supplied to system** | **Fixed constraints (immutable contract)** | **Degrees of freedom (search space)** | **System output** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Layer 1: point assistance** | Human task query within existing design context | Complete system architecture, microarchitecture, interfaces, and tool flow | Localized syntax, logic, or scalar estimate for requested task | Isolated candidate artifact (code snippet, testbench, diagnostic report) |
| **Layer 2: container-bound optimization** | Workload, PPA targets, and parameterized architectural template $\Theta$ | Prescribed template, permitted parameter choices, and external interfaces | Parameter vector $\theta \in \Theta$ (e.g., capacities, unroll factors, macro coordinates) | Best configuration found, $\theta^* \in \Theta$, within prescribed parameterization |
| **Layer 3: AI-native design system** | Workload intent, physical PPA constraints, and verification contract | External workload requirements, physical budget, and correctness contract | Joint structural synthesis: microarchitecture, arithmetic representation, dataflow, and software mapping | Co-adapted candidates, evaluation results, and unresolved constraints |
: **Operational layers differ in their input contracts and architectural degrees of freedom.** Each layer states what the human architect holds fixed, which decisions the automated system may reconsider, and what result it returns. {#tbl-operational-layers-input-output tbl-colwidths="[18,22,22,20,18]"}

![**Operational layers differ in what the design system may change.** Each layer opens decisions that the layer below held fixed, shown struck through in the team's specification. (a) Layer 1 drafts one block inside a frozen design, and the engineer integrates and checks it. (b) Layer 2 searches the parameters of a prescribed template $\Theta$ in a closed loop. (c) Layer 3 opens the template itself, revising hardware and software together under physical evaluation. Evaluation fidelity is separate from this scope: each layer can use analytical models, simulation, or implementation checks appropriate to its claims.](images/fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration){#fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration width="100%" fig-alt="Diagram in which three stacked rows show the operational layers, with Layer 1 at the bottom and Layer 3 at the top. Each row lists what the team specifies, what the system works on, and the feedback it receives, and decisions the team no longer fixes appear struck through. Point assistance drafts one block inside a frozen pipeline for an engineer to integrate, container-bound optimization searches cache capacity, buffer depth, and macro placement within a fixed template, and an AI-native design system revises the compiler schedule, instruction extensions, arithmetic format, and buffering together under physical evaluation."}

Each layer in @fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration is defined by what it releases from the team's specification. In Layer 1 the team has fixed every structural decision, from pipeline topology to bus protocols, and the request is a single block inside that frozen design. The drafted block returns to an engineer who reviews it, wires it in, and runs the lint and timing checks, so no loop closes without a person in it. Layer 2 turns a few of those decisions into parameters, such as subsystem sizes or macro placement, and lets simulator or EDA feedback close a search loop over them, while the template that defines those parameters stays exactly as the team wrote it. Layer 3 releases the template itself: interfaces, pipeline organization, memory hierarchy, and arithmetic become open choices, and the compiler schedule can change with them, yet the workload requirements, physical budget, and correctness contract remain the team's to set.

Moving the boundary of what the system may change does not relax how its candidates are judged (@fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration). Scope and evaluation fidelity answer different questions: a Layer 1 assistant can inspect a post-route timing report while the engineer decides what to edit next, and a Layer 2 optimizer can run full physical implementation inside a fixed template. Conversely, permitting a Layer 3 workflow to revise hardware and software interfaces together does not by itself establish an AI-native capability. Every candidate still has to pass the functional, timing, and physical checks that its intended use demands.

Just as the three layers are independent of evaluation fidelity, they are also distinct from the method families used inside each step. Prediction, generation, and optimization work across all three layers: a predictor estimates performance or physical cost, a generator drafts concrete artifacts (such as RTL modules, configurations, or compiler schedules), and an optimizer searches parameter or decision spaces to improve an objective, while an agent is a software component that reads tool feedback and chooses successive actions in a closed loop without a human between steps. The operational layers specify *which design decisions the workflow may revisit*, whereas method families specify *how each step is carried out* (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization).[^fn-level2-vs-level3-c01] Because each layer fits a different class of problem, a well-scoped parameter search is often better served by a Layer 2 optimizer than by an open-ended Layer 3 system.

[^fn-level2-vs-level3-c01]: **Layer 2 parameter sweeps versus Layer 3 structural adaptation**: Layer 2 workflows explore parameters $\theta \in \Theta$ within a prescribed architectural template. Changing pipeline depth remains Layer 2 when that choice is already encoded in the generator. Layer 3 permits coordinated revisions beyond the template, such as replacing a cache interface with software-managed transfers and adapting the compiler schedule to match. The distinction concerns the permitted formulation, not whether two generated netlists have identical graphs.

### Judging Candidates Against Physical Ground Truth {#sec-demonstration-ceiling}

Classifying what a system may change leaves open the harder question of how it judges what it produces. A generative model trained on human-written hardware descriptions learns to emulate its training corpus, reproducing the stylistic conventions, structural idioms, and historical compromises recorded in existing repositories. Resemblance to human code helps when drafting syntax, but familiarity is not an engineering proof. A candidate block that looks like textbook human RTL may fail timing at real operating corners, while an unfamiliar structure may close timing and meet every power target.

Game-playing systems offer a well-documented precedent for this distinction. AlphaGo combined neural networks first trained to predict moves from human expert games with self-play reinforcement learning and tree search [@SilverEtAl2016AlphaGo], winning its March 2016 match against Lee Sedol 4–1 and playing a second-game move that DeepMind describes as having had about a 1 in 10,000 chance of being played by a human professional [@GoogleDeepMindAlphaGo]. AlphaGo Zero subsequently eliminated human expert games and handcrafted features entirely, learning strictly through self-play under the rules of the game and surpassing the version that defeated Lee Sedol after 36 hours of training [@SilverEtAl2017AlphaGoZero]. A network trained to imitate human experts predicted professional moves more accurately than AlphaGo Zero's network, yet played weaker Go. AlphaGo Master, which started from human games before training further by self-play, won 60 straight online games against top professionals and rated well above AlphaGo Lee, though it still trailed the fully trained AlphaGo Zero (@fig-demonstration-ceiling).

![**Strength followed checks against the rules of the game, not resemblance to human play.** Elo ratings of AlphaGo versions from a single tournament at 5\ s per move [@SilverEtAl2017AlphaGoZero]. Hatched bars mark versions that started from human expert games. AlphaGo Master began from human data and still rated well above AlphaGo Lee, while AlphaGo Zero, trained only by self-play, rated highest.](images/fig-demonstration-ceiling){#fig-demonstration-ceiling width="95%" fig-alt="Horizontal bar chart of Elo ratings for five AlphaGo versions. AlphaGo Zero rates highest at 5,185, followed by AlphaGo Master at 4,858, AlphaGo Lee at 3,739, AlphaGo Fan at 3,144, and the AlphaGo Zero network without search at 3,055. Hatched bars mark the three versions that started from human expert games."}

Every strong version in that progression improved by judging candidate moves against an exact external check, winning games under fixed rules, rather than by how closely its moves matched human play. The same principle applies to computer architecture: human designs remain useful starting points, but candidate hardware must be selected and verified by physical and functional checks rather than by stylistic similarity.

In computer architecture, human-written register-transfer level (RTL) descriptions capture decades of engineering experience, but they also reflect how human teams divide work and manage complexity. Human architects design circuits with modular subsystems, symmetric pipeline stages, and standardized bus protocols (such as Arm's Advanced Microcontroller Bus Architecture (AMBA) Advanced eXtensible Interface (AXI), TileLink, or Coherent Hub Interface) partly because people must inspect, verify, and debug those structures, and partly because modular interfaces enable independent clock-domain crossing (CDC) verification, bounded formal property checks, scan-chain insertion for manufacturing test, and late-cycle engineering change orders. Because a model trained exclusively on human code inherits these structural templates without their physical rationale, it can generate familiar building blocks yet cannot independently distinguish which regularities represent hard physical necessities and which are historical habits that unnecessarily constrain the design space.

The Architecture 2.0 objective is to supply an architectural analogue to the board rules: physical and functional ground truth. Rather than evaluating a proposed circuit by how closely it resembles human code, an AI-native workflow evaluates candidates against execution simulators, static timing analysis (STA), power models, and design rule checking (DRC) tools.[^fn-drc-c01] Bounded Layer 2 optimizers already close loops around such signals, but only within a human-frozen container. A learned macro placer, for example, searches block coordinates within a fixed netlist against a proxy cost built from wirelength, density, and congestion estimates, and whether its gains on that proxy carry through to routed power, performance, and area remains disputed [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement; @ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment]. The Layer 3 objective extends closed-loop physical evaluation to the architectural structure and abstraction contracts themselves, so that measured timing, power, and area decide which unfamiliar microarchitectures survive.

[^fn-drc-c01]: **Design rule checking (DRC)**: Physical verification that inspects geometric layout masks against foundry manufacturing limits, verifying minimum wire spacing, metal widths, enclosure rules, and antenna ratios. A reported violation identifies geometry that fails a rule in the selected runset and requires correction or an accepted waiver. Such rules address manufacturing risks, including metal bridging, open circuits, and yield loss; neither a violation nor a clean report alone determines the outcome of fabrication.

In silicon, the architectural equivalent of AlphaGo's unconventional second-game move is a candidate that departs from human design habits, using asymmetric memory partitioning, non-power-of-two FIFO depths, non-standard instruction packings, or custom datapath staging. An engineer might question such a structure during code review as unidiomatic, yet static timing analysis and physical implementation may show that it achieves better power, performance, and area (PPA) trade-offs. Such a departure earns its place only after downstream checks validate it. Logic equivalence checking must confirm that the implementation matches its specification, CDC analysis must find its crossings safe, scan insertion must succeed, and routing must satisfy the required design rules, with any accepted waivers recorded. Until a candidate passes these checks, its unconventional structure demonstrates nothing about architectural validity.

The Go comparison also highlights an essential physical distinction between games and semiconductor engineering. The rules of Go provide inexpensive, exact state transitions and terminal scoring. Search and learning still consume substantial compute, and AlphaGo Zero evaluates nonterminal search positions with a learned value network rather than playing every simulation to completion. Semiconductor engineering offers no such convenience. Physical signoff (synthesis, place-and-route, parasitic extraction, and static timing across multi-corner operating envelopes) is computationally expensive, high-dimensional, and governed by continuous trade-off surfaces rather than discrete win-loss outcomes.[^fn-sample-complexity-c01] An AI-native architecture system cannot rely on unguided trial-and-error rollouts from scratch; it requires multi-fidelity evaluation hierarchies, where fast analytical models and learned surrogates screen candidate spaces before invoking expensive signoff engines.

[^fn-sample-complexity-c01]: **Sample complexity and oracle cost**: Tabula rasa reinforcement learning in games benefits from simulated environments generating millions of samples per day at low marginal cost per sample, even though the aggregate compute is large. In contrast, evaluating a nanometer semiconductor design requires static timing, parasitic extraction, and physical design engines whose execution latency and, in commercial flows, license costs make unguided trial-and-error sample-inefficient. In practice, hierarchies of cheaper models screen the candidate space before expensive signoff tools are invoked.

Physical ground truth therefore remains the final check on any proposal, while human architects frame the problem, set the operating envelope, and define the correctness contract that every candidate must satisfy.

### Closing the Loop Between Proposals and Tool Checks

Evaluating candidates against physical tools pays off most when fixing a bottleneck requires coordinated changes across several layers of the stack. Consider an accelerator whose interface requires an entire input array to fit in on-chip memory before execution begins. If that interface stays fixed, an input tensor larger than on-chip memory forces a buffer expansion that exceeds the silicon area budget. A better organization can process the tensor in smaller tiles using an explicit double-buffered scratchpad with direct memory access (DMA) descriptor chaining and streaming first-in, first-out (FIFO) queues.[^fn-double-buffering-dma-c01] Making that change work, however, requires matching updates to the software schedule, memory transfer protocol, and partial-result accumulation. A Layer 2 parameter search over buffer sizes cannot find this design because changing the interface and compiler schedule lies outside its fixed template.

[^fn-double-buffering-dma-c01]: **Double-buffering and descriptor chaining**: Double-buffering ping-pongs between two independent memory banks so that memory transfer into one bank overlaps arithmetic execution on the other. Descriptor chaining allows a direct memory access (DMA) controller to execute non-contiguous, multi-block data transfers autonomously by traversing linked metadata packets in memory without requiring host processor interrupt interventions.

Although human architects routinely devise such cross-layer solutions, the AI-native opportunity is for the design system to synthesize and evaluate these alternatives as the study progresses. A generator constructs the tiled microarchitecture along with matching compiler schedules, while an optimizer tunes tile dimensions and buffer depths. If simulation reveals excessive transfer overhead, the diagnostic feedback directs the next iteration toward a different buffering topology (@fig-architecture-20-loop).

![**Tool feedback guides design generation and revision.** In this proposed loop, a generator constructs a candidate organization and matching hardware and software. Engineering tools evaluate its behavior and implementation. Results guide the next proposal and remain available for architect review.](images/fig-architecture-20-loop){#fig-architecture-20-loop width="90%" fig-alt="Loop diagram in which requirements guide generation of a candidate organization, implementation of matching hardware and software, and engineering evaluations. Measurements and failures return to design generation and remain available for architect review."}

The feedback returning from engineering tools carries rich diagnostic structure rather than a scalar pass/fail grade. Suppose a candidate reduces simulated latency, but physical synthesis reports that signals cannot close timing along an arithmetic critical path. That timing failure rejects the immediate candidate under the current constraints, but the path report also helps diagnose whether logic depth, routing delay, loading, or clock relationships dominate. An automated design system must interpret these contributions to choose an effective repair, such as retiming the pipeline, inserting pipeline stages, restructuring arithmetic trees, or changing placement. Capturing these tool reports in structured representations that preserve their hardware meaning is a central challenge taken up in @sec-data-representations-world-models.

Each experiment refines both the candidate design and the next step of the search. Running those iterations reliably takes substantial engineering infrastructure to keep hardware RTL and software binaries in sync, parse outputs from diverse tools, and recover cleanly from tool crashes. Whether that infrastructure cost is worth paying becomes clear only on a demanding system problem, such as designing a wearable processor under strict power, thermal, and latency limits.

## The Lighthouse Mobile XR Case Study

Evaluating an automated design tool on an isolated arithmetic kernel or a standalone RTL module hides the cross-layer bottlenecks that dominate real silicon programs: a block that looks efficient in a unit testbench can still starve on off-chip memory traffic, stall behind compiler scheduling dependencies, or violate the heat limits of a wearable package. To keep those full-system constraints in view across every chapter, this book uses a running design challenge called the *Lighthouse* project. The task is to design a mobile extended-reality (XR) compute subsystem that runs concurrent perception and rendering workloads within the strict power, thermal, and latency budgets of a wearable device, serving as a shared testbed even though the complete system remains a research target rather than a completed silicon tapeout.

A target does not need to be solved today to focus a field, provided it sets a clear bar for success. The DARPA Grand Challenge offers a familiar precedent: in 2004, not a single autonomous vehicle completed the desert route, yet just one year later five vehicles finished the 132-mile course [@BuehlerEtAl2009DARPA; @ThrunEtAl2006Stanley]. What drove that progress was a shared, objective, and falsifiable milestone. Lighthouse sets a similar target for computer architecture, where generating hardware code is only a first step toward delivering an independently verified, physically realizable chip.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{7\baselineskip}
```

> **The Lighthouse goal.** Demonstrate by 2030 that an AI-native design system can expand a compact system request into candidate implementations spanning software, microarchitecture, and physical layout; quantify their power, performance, and area (PPA) trade-offs; and deliver an implementation that satisfies system requirements and passes physical signoff.

Mobile XR makes those cross-layer trade-offs immediate. A frame delivered past its deadline breaks user immersion even when average throughput is high, and a brief burst of speed is useless if it drives the headset past its thermal limit. Benchmarks such as XRBench [@KwonEtAl2023XRBench] and end-to-end pipelines such as ILLIXR [@HuzaifaEtAl2021ILLIXR] show why isolated microarchitectural tweaks rarely suffice: cutting memory traffic has to match how the compiler schedules each frame, and peak compute throughput has to stay within skin-temperature limits. We can state the Lighthouse challenge as the compact request a design team might hand an automated system:

```{=latex}
\Needspace{12\baselineskip}
```

::: {.callout-lighthouse}
Design a low-power, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for an XRBench-class real-time mobile XR workload. The implementation may use a vector-capable central processing unit (CPU), an accelerator, or a system-on-chip (SoC) block. It must target a 3\ W thermal design power (TDP) envelope in a 3\ nm-class low-power mobile process.

Return a design-space report that explains which candidates were tested, how they compared, and which design the team should investigate further.
:::

The Lighthouse prompt is intentionally brief. It names a workload class and top-level physical targets, but leaves the core microarchitecture, memory hierarchy, and software runtime open. Those unstated choices span the eight coupled domains in @fig-moonshot-prompt, and each choice determines which simulators, implementation tools, and verification checks are needed to evaluate a candidate design.

<!-- arch2-allow: figure-placement-override The print-size diagram needs flexible float placement to stay near the Lighthouse prompt. -->
![**A compact request leaves many architectural decisions open.** The Lighthouse prompt expands into eight coupled domains. Choices in those domains determine which workload simulations, implementation tools, and verification checks are needed to evaluate a candidate.](images/fig-moonshot-prompt){#fig-moonshot-prompt width="100%" fig-pos="!htbp" fig-alt="Diagram in which the Lighthouse prompt expands into workload, ISA and ABI, compute, memory, power, software, process, and verification decisions, which feed design experiments and engineering review."}

Rather than a finished specification, those eight domains are design questions the architect or design system has to answer beyond the prompt's 64-bit RISC-V baseline, 3\ W power ceiling, and 3\ nm-class process:

1. **Workload domain.** Identify the specific XRBench kernels, inputs, and execution traces the subsystem must run [@KwonEtAl2023XRBench]. A design tuned for visual-inertial odometry alone may stall when neural rendering and depth reconstruction contend for the same memory bandwidth.
2. **ISA and ABI contract domain.** Select instruction set extensions and the application binary interface (ABI) that governs register conventions and parameter passing.[^fn-abi-c01] Adding the RISC-V vector (RVV) extension is an architectural trade-off that has to be measured [@RISCV2026UnprivilegedISA]: wider vector registers enlarge the state an operating system may need to save and restore on context switches, depending on how often tasks use vectors and how the kernel manages that state [@RISCV2026PrivilegedISA].
3. **Compute organization domain.** Decide how to divide work across general-purpose vector cores, neural processing units (NPUs), and fixed-function engines. An NPU built as a systolic array streams data across a regular grid of processing elements,[^fn-systolic-array-c01] so its efficiency depends on whether the compiler can tile tensors to keep data moving without starving the array boundaries.
4. **Memory and data movement domain.** Size the memory hierarchy, on-chip buffers, and interconnect bandwidth. A baseline might combine private caches, a shared last-level cache, and tightly coupled memory (TCM) scratchpads.[^fn-tcm-scratchpad-c01] Larger caches cut off-chip DRAM traffic, but they take up die area and can add access latency and static leakage, so the evaluation must weigh both effects inside the 3\ W budget.
5. **Power and thermal envelope domain.** Define what counts inside the 3\ W budget and how long the chip must sustain it. A skin-temperature limit turns power into a packaging problem: dissipating 3\ W in a passively cooled eyeglass temple is much harder than dissipating the same power in a tethered pack or an actively cooled headset.[^fn-xr-glasses-thermal-c01] Thermal models have to check whether the chosen package and placement can actually carry that heat away.
6. **Compiler and runtime stack domain.** Specify how software schedules work across hardware units. While a 120\ frames per second (FPS) display rate sets an 8.33\ ms frame interval, the runtime must also meet the individual latency deadlines and dependencies of perception, pose estimation, and rendering, which can be pipelined across frames rather than sharing a single serial budget [@HuzaifaEtAl2021ILLIXR]. Because a custom accelerator adds no system value if compiler schedules leave it waiting on pipeline dependencies, hardware organization and runtime schedules must be evaluated together.
7. **Physical constraints domain.** Select the standard cell libraries, memory compilers, and operating corners. Calling a process "3\ nm-class" names a technology generation, whereas synthesis and place-and-route tools require concrete foundry Liberty timing libraries and metal layer stacks.
8. **Reliability and verification domain.** Set the correctness contracts and operating corners that a design must pass. Functional behavior, bus protocol compliance, clock-domain crossings, and power-state transitions each require their own verification checks.

[^fn-abi-c01]: **Application binary interface (ABI)**: While an instruction set architecture (ISA) specifies machine instruction semantics, the ABI governs runtime conventions including caller- versus callee-saved register allocation, parameter passing, and stack alignment. These conventions set how much register state a function call must preserve. Operating system context switches are a separate cost, governed by how much architectural state the ISA defines (for example, the vector register file) and by whether the kernel saves it eagerly or lazily.

[^fn-systolic-array-c01]: **Systolic arrays**: A two-dimensional spatial grid of processing elements that stream data directly to immediate neighbors on rhythmic clock cycles, maximizing weight and activation reuse while eliminating repeated register-file read energy. Arithmetic efficiency drops sharply when tensor dimensions do not tile evenly across the grid or when memory bandwidth fails to sustain boundary data ingestion.

[^fn-tcm-scratchpad-c01]: **Tightly coupled memory (TCM)**: An on-chip static random-access memory (SRAM) block mapped directly into the physical memory address space, providing predictable access latency under its declared arbitration and access conditions. Unlike hardware-managed caches, scratchpads rely on software or DMA to orchestrate data transfers, eliminating tag-check energy overhead and non-deterministic cache-miss latency in real-time deadlines.

[^fn-xr-glasses-thermal-c01]: **Mobile XR and Smart Glasses Thermal Boundaries**: A power target alone does not determine the temperature of a wearable surface. Heat paths through the package and frame, ambient conditions, and duration of operation affect the temperature where the device contacts skin, and product-safety standards limit that temperature for prolonged contact. The study must select an enclosure, define its allowed surface temperature and contact conditions, and establish whether it can sustain the power target. A tethered compute unit or actively cooled head-mounted display changes the heat paths and therefore the feasible operating envelope.

Decisions in one domain quickly surface as physical or protocol constraints in another. When an accelerator connects to an AMBA AXI crossbar, for example, its controller must obey handshake rules even when downstream memory channels stall [@Arm2020AXI]. Backpressure (when the receiver deasserts `READY` while `VALID` remains asserted) requires the sender to hold its data stable.[^fn-axi-backpressure-c01] A generated controller that mishandles backpressure can look fast in an isolated unit testbench that never stalls, yet lock up the system bus as soon as the SoC experiences real memory traffic. Performance numbers mean little until verification exercises those boundary protocols under load.

[^fn-axi-backpressure-c01]: **AXI protocol handshakes**: On-chip AMBA AXI interconnects govern data transfers through paired `VALID` (producer) and `READY` (consumer) control signals across independent address, read, and write channels. Backpressure occurs when a consumer deasserts `READY`, forcing the producer to hold data stable; failing to handle backpressure in generated controllers causes data corruption, dropped packets, or system-level bus deadlocks.

Because the eight domains are coupled so tightly, tuning a single parameter inside a fixed template, such as sweeping cache capacity in an unchanged hierarchy, reaches diminishing returns quickly. Larger gains come from testing whether a different organization altogether, such as replacing hardware-managed caches with software-scheduled scratchpads and DMA descriptor streaming, fits the 3\ W budget better. Even then, a study does not have to search all eight domains at once. Instead, the architect picks a focused question, holds the surrounding interfaces fixed, and opens only the degrees of freedom needed to answer it, turning an open-ended prompt into an executable specification that tools can actually run.

## Turning Design Goals into Executable Specifications {#sec-intent-vs-spec}

If a team hands the two-paragraph Lighthouse prompt straight to an automated search tool, the run either stalls immediately on missing input traces and cell libraries, or exploits holes in the problem statement, such as shrinking on-chip memory to meet the 3\ W target on paper while pushing uncounted DRAM traffic outside the simulation boundary. Preventing those failures requires an executable specification that translates high-level design intent into the exact configurations, workloads, and checks that simulators and synthesis tools run. Suppose the Lighthouse team wants to test whether co-designing the memory hierarchy and software tiling can meet the frame deadlines within the 3\ W envelope. Out of the eight domains in @fig-moonshot-prompt, the executable specification states which parameters are held fixed, which are allowed to vary, and which measurements decide whether a candidate succeeds.

Five practical decisions define that setup:

1. **Pin down the workloads and correctness checks.** Choose a specific XRBench kernel, realistic input traces, and a reference behavioral model. Because loop tiling changes the order of floating-point operations and memory accesses, verification has to confirm that tiled outputs match reference golden outputs within declared numerical tolerances. Under a 120\ FPS target, the specification also has to separate the 8.33\ ms frame interval from per-stage deadlines and end-to-end motion-to-photon latency.
2. **State which architectural parameters can move.** In this experiment, memory capacities, scratchpad banking, tile dimensions, and DMA descriptor queues vary together, while the ISA and application interfaces stay fixed. Because each hardware candidate needs matching compiler schedules, writing or updating those compiler lowering passes is part of the engineering cost of the study (@sec-feedback-verification-trust).
3. **Set physical accounting boundaries.** State exactly which on-chip blocks and off-chip memory interfaces count toward the 3\ W power budget, which activity traces drive dynamic power estimation, and how long the workload must run so that offloaded data movement is charged to the design. Calibrated thermal models then check whether the package and cooling setup keep surface temperatures within limits.
4. **Connect evaluation tools across fidelity levels.** Cycle-accurate simulation measures throughput and memory stalls, while logic synthesis and place-and-route tools test whether a candidate closes timing and fits the area budget. Those physical checks require foundry process design kits (PDKs),[^fn-pdk-c01] characterized standard cell libraries,[^fn-liberty-corners-c01] and multi-corner timing constraints.
5. **Fix baselines, Pareto frontiers, and stopping rules.** Compare co-designed candidates against matched baselines that tune only memory size or only software tiling, so the team can tell whether changing both together actually buys anything. Plotting feasible designs on a Pareto frontier shows which candidates cannot improve one metric without hurting another [@Deb2001MultiObjective], and a fixed compute budget stops the search from running indefinitely.

[^fn-pdk-c01]: **Process design kit (PDK)**: The package for one manufacturing process that supplies device models, design rules, and related data used by implementation tools. The open SKY130 PDK demonstrates that a PDK can be published [@SkyWater2020SKY130PDK], but it cannot supply the authorized project-specific information for a different process or commercial tool flow.

[^fn-liberty-corners-c01]: **Characterized cell libraries**: Tabulated databases (typically in Liberty `.lib` format) generated from low-level Simulation Program with Integrated Circuit Emphasis (SPICE) simulations that record the propagation delay, transition time, and leakage power of standard logic cells across discrete process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) operating corners.

Putting those five choices on record makes the experiment reproducible regardless of how it turns out: the study may find a worthwhile co-designed memory system, show that a simpler cache tweak is enough, or prove with solid evidence (rather than an exhausted compute budget) that the target constraints cannot all be met at once. And because a design method has to be judged by what it costs to run, the record must track not only the winning candidate's PPA, but also the total engineering effort spent setting up, searching, and verifying the space.

Language models can help draft this specification early on by pulling candidate constraints out of product documents, catching mismatched units, or pointing out ambiguous timing deadlines. Still, a human architect has to review and sign off on the specification before any search begins. Once the specification is locked in, the work shifts from drafting a single artifact to running a closed-loop design system that proposes candidates, invokes tools, and learns from their measurements.

## Isolated AI Models versus Closed-Loop Design Systems

When an engineer prompts a standalone language model for RTL or cache sizes without an execution harness, the output is an untested guess: without deterministic compilation, simulation, and provenance binding, candidate proposals either fail to build or quietly drift across incompatible tool flags. A model's learned weights capture statistical patterns from training data, not the state of the current project, such as which workload trace to run, which PDK to target, or which power ceiling defines a passing result. While a standalone model can draft logic, predict power dissipation, or rank configurations for simulation, running an architecture study requires a closed-loop design system.

That distinction still holds for an architecture foundation model, a pretrained model that can be adapted across tasks [@BommasaniEtAl2021FoundationModels] to draft RTL, estimate physical metrics, or summarize tool logs. The surrounding design system is what ties those capabilities to physical reality: it manages the execution environment, pairs generated hardware with compiled software binaries, runs deterministic EDA tools, and records what they measure, calling on analytical models and conventional optimizers whenever they beat learned approximations.

In our Lighthouse memory study, for instance, the design system has to generate a matching hardware configuration and software schedule, launch the cycle-accurate simulator on the chosen XR trace, parse the resulting log, and attach the measured stall cycles to that exact candidate so the next proposal can build on the result (@fig-foundation-system).

![**A model contributes to an experiment run by the surrounding design system.** The current requirements, design versions, and tool configurations supply the context for proposals and evaluations. Learned and conventional methods use the returned results to select further experiments. Reusable knowledge in a model remains separate from the inputs and results of the current study [@ReddiYazdanbakhsh2025Architecture20].](images/fig-foundation-system){#fig-foundation-system width="90%" fig-alt="System diagram in which requirements, matching hardware and software versions, and tool settings provide inputs to learned or conventional methods and engineering tools. Results are saved with the candidate that produced them and can guide the next experiment. A foundation model is one optional component."}

Keeping that context attached to every measurement is what makes a comparison trustworthy. Suppose a proposed cache configuration appears to speed up the workload. Before accepting that result, the team has to verify that the candidate and the baseline ran the exact same trace length, compiler optimization flags, and memory timing model; a bare claim that one design was "faster" means nothing without the setup that produced it.

For that reason, the design system must save every candidate architecture, software schedule, and tool configuration as a versioned artifact paired with its execution record, including input datasets, model checkpoints, random seeds, and tool versions (@sec-architecture-20-ontology). With that provenance in place, engineers can audit unexpected wins, reproduce failures, and tell whether an improvement came from a better model or a quiet change in the evaluation harness.

## Judging Whether an Architectural Gain Is Real

Provenance tells us how a measurement was produced; the next step is deciding what that measurement says about the architecture question. In the Lighthouse memory study, the question is whether co-designing the memory hierarchy and software tiling can meet the frame deadlines within the 3\ W power envelope and die-area budget, and each tool run tests only one piece of that claim.

If a larger cache cuts simulated frame latency but blows past the area budget during floorplanning, the experiment has still done useful work by exposing a physical bottleneck. The team can now drop that candidate, try a different banking layout, or ask whether finer software tiling can get by with a smaller buffer. Reporting the simulated speedup while leaving out the area failure would hide the very constraint that should drive the next iteration.

### Matching the Claim to the Tool That Tested It

An automated search can easily mistake a favorable early estimate for a finished chip, treating a back-of-the-envelope analytical formula or a fast learned power predictor as proof that a candidate will route cleanly and close timing at signoff. Preventing that error requires separating three things in every experiment: the *candidate* (the specific hardware–software configuration under test), the *artifacts* that tools build from it (RTL source, gate netlists, floorplans, software binaries, and their measurements), and the *architectural conclusion* that those measurements actually support. Because each tool observes the design at a different level of detail, any reported metric has to state the fidelity level that produced it.

In practice, evaluation moves through three levels of increasing fidelity and cost:

1. **Analytical screening bounds.** Fast closed-form equations rule out impossible designs before a simulator ever launches: Amdahl's law caps the end-to-end speedup from accelerating a single kernel [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor], and the Roofline model caps achievable throughput for a given operational intensity and memory bandwidth [@Williams2009Roofline]. Candidates that cannot meet targets even under these optimistic bounds can be discarded immediately.
2. **Learned surrogate models.** Trained surrogates estimate expensive physical metrics, such as macro wirelength or dynamic power, at a tiny fraction of the runtime of commercial EDA tools [@ForresterSobesterKeane2008Surrogate]. Because a surrogate reflects only the variables in its training set, however, an optimizer driven solely by a power surrogate may pack memory macros so tightly that the chip becomes unroutable during place-and-route.[^fn-overfitting-c01]
3. **Simulation and physical signoff checks.** Candidates that survive early screening still have to pass slow, authoritative tools. Cycle-level simulation measures execution latency and cache miss rates on real traces, while manufacturing readiness requires full physical signoff: static timing closure across all required operating corners, layout-versus-schematic (LVS) agreement, geometric design rule checks (DRC), and power-grid voltage drop (IR-drop) analysis.[^fn-physical-signoff-c01]

[^fn-physical-signoff-c01]: **Physical signoff**: The definitive certification milestone required before releasing mask data for semiconductor fabrication (tapeout). Signoff mandates static timing closure across all required operating corners, layout-versus-schematic (LVS) consistency, geometric design rule checks (DRC), and power-grid voltage drop (IR-drop) analysis using the tools, models, and rule decks accepted by the target foundry or fabrication service.

[^fn-overfitting-c01]: **Overfitting and Proxy Exploitation**: The machine-learning failure of fitting the noise of a training sample so closely that performance does not generalize to new data [@HastieTibshiraniFriedman2009Elements]. Proxy exploitation is analogous but distinct; it occurs when search algorithms exploit omissions or modeling errors in an evaluator, embodying Goodhart's law in automated design [@Strathern1997Goodhart; @Goodhart1975MonetaryManagement].

Even a high-fidelity tool is only as good as the test or check it runs. If a generator drafts both an accelerator block and its unit testbench from the same ambiguous prompt, both files can share the same misunderstanding of the specification and report a 100% pass rate on a broken design. Just as the Knight–Leveson multiversion programming experiments showed that independent teams often make correlated errors when working from the same specification [@KnightLeveson1986Multiversion], a generated testbench in our tiled accelerator study that checks one tile at a time will miss synchronization deadlocks that appear only when multiple tiles accumulate partial sums together. A trustworthy evaluation record therefore has to state not only which checks passed, but which behaviors were never tested (@sec-feedback-verification-trust).

### Design Quality and Engineering Effort {#sec-efficiency-claims-need-rejectable-loops}

A single metric can be just as misleading when it ignores the rest of the chip. In the Lighthouse subsystem, speeding up arithmetic units does more harm than good if it triggers extra off-chip DRAM traffic, since moving data across package pins burns orders of magnitude more energy than an on-chip floating-point operation [@HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach]. Any credible comparison has to account for total energy across the full workload within the 3\ W budget (@sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales).

That same full-system accounting applies to the design process itself. Judging an AI-native design method requires separating two records:

1. **Design quality:** The physical PPA metrics of the resulting chip (clock frequency, dynamic and leakage power, die area, and thermal margins).
2. **Engineering effort:** The total human and machine cost spent to reach that chip (compute hours, EDA tool licenses, discarded runs, prompt tuning, and manual debugging).

A search tool that finds a slightly faster microarchitecture by burning millions of simulator hours or weeks of human testbench repair has not made the team more productive. Keeping both records visible lets engineers see whether a better chip came from a smarter method or simply from spending more compute and staff time.

Project schedules obey the same arithmetic. Because writing initial RTL takes up only a small slice of a chip project's timeline, speeding up code generation alone cannot dramatically shorten time to tapeout; Amdahl's law constrains design teams just as strictly as it constrains parallel processors.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Verification share of project time for the Amdahl callout, read from
# data/datasets/chapter7-wilson-verification-scissors-gap.csv (Wilson Research Group
# printed means, 2010-2020). The drafting ceiling and speedup bound are computed here.
import csv as _csv_c01
from pathlib import Path as _Path_c01
import _python.plots as _ap_c01

_wilson_path = (_Path_c01(_ap_c01.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
                / "data" / "datasets" / "chapter7-wilson-verification-scissors-gap.csv")
with open(_wilson_path, encoding="utf-8") as _fh:
    _wilson = [r for r in _csv_c01.DictReader(l for l in _fh if not l.startswith("#"))
               if r["avg_pct_project_time_in_verification"]]
_verif = [float(r["avg_pct_project_time_in_verification"]) for r in _wilson]
verif_share_min = min(_verif)
verif_share_max = max(_verif)
verif_year_lo = min(int(r["study_year"]) for r in _wilson)
verif_year_hi = max(int(r["study_year"]) for r in _wilson)
drafting_share_max = 100 - verif_share_min
drafting_speedup_max = 1 / (1 - drafting_share_max / 100)
```

::: {.callout-law title="Amdahl's Law for Semiconductor Teams"}
**The classical principle.** If a fraction $f$ of the original work is accelerated by a factor $s$ and the rest is unchanged, the overall speedup is $S = \frac{1}{(1-f) + f/s}$ [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor]. The expression assumes that the original allocation remains applicable and that the acceleration introduces no additional overhead.

**A bound from survey data.** In the Wilson Research Group studies from `{python} verif_year_lo` to `{python} verif_year_hi`, the mean share of project time spent in verification never fell below `{python} f'{verif_share_min:.0f}'`% [@Foster2013WilsonPart5; @Foster2021WilsonPart8]. If a project follows that mean allocation and the work is treated as nonoverlapping, RTL drafting occupies only part of the remaining time, so its share $f$ is at most `{python} f'{drafting_share_max:.0f}'`%. Even instantaneous drafting then gives $S_{\text{max}} = 1/(1-f) \le$ `{python} f'{drafting_speedup_max:.1f}'`$\times$ under these assumptions, and accounting for architecture design, physical implementation, and review shrinks the drafting share further. A real project must therefore measure its own time breakdown, including any extra downstream verification caused by generated code, and identify which overlapping tasks actually sit on the critical path.

**The architectural consequence.** Larger gains require reducing work outside drafting or changing the workflow itself. Coordinating hardware and software changes is one possible way to improve the search, but building and checking that coordination also takes work. The broader workflow interpretation is developed in @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes.
:::

Testing whether an AI-native workflow actually helps on a problem like Lighthouse therefore requires comparing it against a strong conventional baseline given the same specification, EDA tools, and compute budget, with success criteria fixed *before* the search begins. Fair accounting also has to include the amortized engineering work spent building the design system itself (prompt tuning, model fine-tuning, tool wrappers, and harness testing) so that setup labor is not quietly left off the books.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Credit a design method only for a better result or a lower total cost"}
**The principle:** Judge a design method against a credible alternative given the same task, tool access, and budget. It earns credit only when it improves the architecture result, reduces the total effort of reaching a comparable result, or both.

**The application:** Fix the comparison criteria before either search begins, and count the effort spent preparing the design system (model adaptation, tool integration, test development) as well as running it. A better candidate can establish a quality gain within a matched budget, but it does not by itself establish a reduction in engineering cost.
:::

Together, these rules give us three plain questions to ask of any published design-automation result: which architectural parameters was the method allowed to change, what did implementation and verification tools actually prove about the resulting chip, and what did the complete workflow cost in compute and engineering time? A tool does not need to solve the entire Lighthouse challenge to be useful, as long as we state clearly which piece of the job it handles and where its evaluation stops.

## What Published Systems Can and Cannot Do Yet {#sec-data-scarcity-verification-load}

Three published efforts in hardware-description generation, learned macro placement, and commercial accelerator design show how those three questions clarify what current methods accomplish and where their evaluation stops.

At the module-drafting level, VerilogEval pairs standardized programming prompts with unit testbenches for generated hardware descriptions [@VerilogEval; @PinckneyEtAl2024RevisitingVerilogEval]. Its code-completion and specification-to-RTL tasks test whether a language model can emit syntactically valid Verilog that passes functional checks, using the Pass@1 metric to estimate the probability that a single generated candidate passes its unit testbench under declared sampling parameters.[^fn-pass-at-k-c01] While a high Pass@1 score provides useful evidence when choosing a model for local RTL drafting, it establishes only that isolated modules pass behavioral unit tests; it says nothing about microarchitectural efficiency, clock-domain-crossing safety, or physical timing closure.

[^fn-pass-at-k-c01]: **Pass@k metric**: Originating in software code-generation benchmarks, Pass@k measures the statistical probability that at least one of $k$ generated code candidates passes a functional unit testbench. In hardware design, passing a behavioral testbench does not establish that the Verilog is synthesizable, avoids inferred latches, satisfies clock-domain-crossing safety, or meets physical timing constraints.

At the physical floorplanning stage, learned macro placement optimizes the $(x,y)$ spatial coordinates of circuit macros within a fixed gate netlist [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]. Because the optimizer searches inside an established netlist, it represents a Layer 2 capability: its evaluation measures floorplan search efficiency within fixed structural boundaries, without altering bus topologies, memory partitioning, or software runtime scheduling. In a broader AI-native workflow, congestion feedback from macro placement could point to a microarchitectural bottleneck, but another component would have to propose and synthesize those cross-layer revisions.

Industrial projects have begun combining several such tools within a single chip program. OpenAI reported that machine learning assisted the development of its custom inference accelerator, Jalapeño, helping move the project from initial design to tapeout in nine months while optimizing arithmetic units [@OpenAI2026JalapenoFirstResults]. Trade reports noted that the team reached first silicon in under twenty months with an internal staff averaging fewer than one hundred people, excluding its partner Broadcom, though combined staffing and total engineering cost were not disclosed [@Smith2026JalapenoIEEE]. While neither account constitutes a controlled peer-reviewed experiment, three reported practices clarify how the effort maps onto the operational layers:

1. **Design entry through high-level synthesis.** The team wrote logic in Google's open-source XLS (Accelerated Hardware Synthesis) framework using DSLX or C++ before compiling to Verilog. Software-like representations reduced syntactic complexity for code-generation models, though no controlled comparison against handwritten RTL was reported.
2. **Specialized physical design partnership.** OpenAI focused on microarchitecture and high-level synthesis, while Broadcom carried physical signoff from gate netlists through tapeout. The team's Hot Chips presentation, as described in the trade report, attributed a 10\% matrix-unit area reduction to AI-guided optimization over an optimized human baseline [@Smith2026JalapenoIEEE].
3. **Model-generated kernels post-silicon.** After silicon bring-up, internal models generated optimized assembly kernels for frontier models. On DeepSeek's multi-head latent attention (MLA) kernel, efficiency rose from 0.31\% to 88.94\% of the theoretical ceiling set by compute and memory bandwidth in roughly forty hours [@Smith2026JalapenoIEEE]. OpenAI separately reported that generated kernels for specific GPT-OSS attention and mixture-of-experts blocks outperformed existing expert implementations by 1.5$\times$ to 1.8$\times$ [@OpenAI2026JalapenoFirstResults].

These results show what an engineering team can accomplish by combining automated point tools across a project, yet each technique still operated within a bounded container: drafting logic in a high-level language (Layer 1), floorplanning a partitioned netlist (Layer 2), or tuning software kernels on fixed silicon (Layer 2). Neither account describes a closed loop in which downstream physical timing or post-silicon bottlenecks fed back to revise upstream microarchitectural interfaces, or compares total engineering cost against a matched conventional baseline. As a result, these reports do not establish a complete Layer 3 capability or measure its value against that baseline.

Once a workflow reaches beyond those bounded containers, technical capability is no longer the only limit. An optimizer can rearrange macro coordinates or tune compiler flags on its own, whereas repartitioning an on-chip memory hierarchy changes power envelopes, software runtimes, and product requirements. Any organization deploying a broader exploration system must therefore decide which choices belong inside an automated loop and which require human architectural signoff.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
```

## Human Review and Design Decisions {#sec-from-architecture-10-to-architecture-20}

An automated exploration system can launch simulations, draft candidate RTL, and check power estimates within the experimental boundaries set by the architect, but it cannot rewrite those boundaries when a search stalls. A tool authorized to search memory hierarchies within a 3\ W budget has no authority to raise that power limit when no candidate converges.

In our Lighthouse study, for example, a candidate that reduces simulated memory stall cycles before static timing or thermal checks finish can stay in the active Pareto pool while the harness queues those downstream runs. If synthesis later exposes a timing violation, the system can try automated retiming or test alternative banking schemes within its declared scope. Once closing timing requires relaxing frame latency or increasing supply voltage, however, human architects must step in, because trading product requirements against system margins and commercial risk lies outside what an automated tool can decide.

People also remain accountable for turning empirical measurements into final design commitments. Domain specialists inspect physical signoff reports and validate functional testbenches, while engineering leaders decide whether to authorize mask tapeout. Automation organizes candidate exploration and maps Pareto trade-offs, but responsibility for irreversible commitments to silicon rests with the human team.

That responsibility requires reviewers to examine the architectural reasoning behind a candidate rather than merely signing off on clean tool logs. When an automated system recommends replacing a cache with a scratchpad, the architect still has to ask why alternative compiler schedules fell short, whether the workload assumptions match real operating conditions, and which physical corner cases remain untested, because a sequence of passing checks in a log file cannot substitute for understanding how the hardware works. @sec-what-architect-owns formalizes this review discipline and shows how architects retain control of technical decisions as design automation scales.

## Assessing Progress Toward the Moonshot

Evaluations of automated chip design often blur technical feasibility, workflow economics, and business outcomes, celebrating an expensive end-to-end demonstration as an engineering productivity win or dismissing a sound optimization method because shifting market priorities canceled a tapeout. Because tool capability, workflow cost, and commercial manufacturing answer different questions, any assessment of progress toward the Architecture 2.0 moonshot must separate three tests:

1. **The engineering milestone:** Can an AI-native system translate a compact specification into a verified, physically realizable design that passes signoff by 2030? This milestone tests end-to-end operational capability across declared workloads, tools, and constraints. A study that proves a specification is physically impossible yields valuable engineering insight, but it does not complete the implementation milestone.
2. **The methodological value:** Does the automated workflow find better architectural trade-offs, reduce total engineering cost, or shorten project schedules compared to a matched conventional baseline? Matching the baseline at equal cost establishes feasibility within the study; improving design quality or lowering total cost gives teams a reason to adopt the method within that assessed scope.
3. **The tapeout decision:** Should the resulting design be manufactured in silicon? That decision weighs market timing, foundry wafer costs, package assembly yields, and business risk tolerance. A team might reasonably choose not to manufacture an exceptional research design, or might tape out a candidate found through an expensive, suboptimal search if market deadlines demand it.

When we keep these three evaluations distinct, research progress can be measured with scientific rigor rather than shifting goalposts after experiments conclude.

## How the Rest of This Book Is Organized

The chapters ahead examine both the architectural bottlenecks behind those three tests and the automated design methods built to address them. Assuming familiarity with core computer architecture and introducing machine learning, formal verification, and physical signoff concepts as they are used (with reading paths detailed in the Preface), the book progresses through three parts. It first diagnoses why manual design loops no longer scale and defines the six-stage Architecture 2.0 life cycle (@sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales and @sec-architecture-20-ontology). It then builds the core engineering machinery: structured design-state records (@sec-data-representations-world-models), prediction, generation, and optimization methods (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization), reproducible tool harnesses (@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces), and the verification checks that test what those tools return (@sec-feedback-verification-trust). Finally, it examines how closed-loop patterns transfer across the stack (@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack), how to evaluate complete workflows under adversarial tests and matched budgets (@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect), what decisions human architects must own (@sec-what-architect-owns), and what shared open infrastructure the field needs to build next (@sec-bootstrapping-ecosystem).

## Open Questions

Each chapter concludes with open research questions that define active frontiers in AI-native computer architecture:

- **When a short prompt leaves out key system details, how can a design tool tell which missing numbers will actually change the hardware?** A brief specification such as our Lighthouse prompt says nothing about memory ordering, thermal time constants, or tail-latency limits. If the system fills in those blanks silently, it may spend days optimizing the wrong product; if it stops to ask the human architect about every unspecified parameter, automation loses its value. We still lack fast ways to estimate how sensitive downstream power, performance, and area (PPA) are to missing specifications before invoking slow implementation tools, so that the system brings only the ambiguities that shift the Pareto frontier to the architect.
- **How can we verify unconventional microarchitectures that step outside familiar human design templates?** Human architects rely on symmetric pipeline stages, power-of-two buffer capacities, and standard bus handshakes partly because those regular idioms keep mental models and formal verification tractable. An AI-native design system guided directly by physical tool feedback could propose asymmetric memory hierarchies or irregular datapath staging that outperform human templates, much as self-play discovered unfamiliar strategies in Go. For such non-standard topologies to survive engineering signoff, however, the generator cannot stop at emitting register-transfer logic; it must also produce machine-checkable interface invariants, clock-domain-crossing proofs, and scan-chain structures that verification tools can audit.
- **When a chip fails timing or routing late in physical design, how do we trace that failure back to the microarchitectural or compiler choice that caused it?** Static timing analysis and place-and-route tools report problems in physical coordinates, such as picoseconds of setup violation along a congested metal layer or localized voltage droop across a macro row. To fix the root cause rather than merely perturbing tool seeds, the workflow has to translate those physical symptoms into an upstream change, such as repartitioning a scratchpad bank, altering an instruction pipeline, or restructuring a compiler loop schedule. Because synthesis, placement, and routing lower a design through discrete transformations with no differentiable gradient, we still lack reliable ways to trace a physical signoff violation back to the right upstream lever.
- **How can we tell ahead of time whether a design problem needs joint Layer 3 co-design rather than separate Layer 2 hardware and software sweeps?** When a search opens hardware and software interfaces at the same time, it multiplies the number of candidate combinations and breaks pre-verified module boundaries, driving up both simulation runtime and verification cost. Before paying that price, architects need analytical or empirical checks that measure cross-layer coupling, such as how strongly compiler tile dimensions interact with on-chip buffer leakage and package thermal limits under a 3\ W envelope, so they can predict whether joint co-design will uncover trade-offs that sequential hardware and software passes cannot reach.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{12\baselineskip}
```

## Summary

The memory-and-tiling walk-through showed how an architectural study moves from local parameter tuning to cross-layer co-design when an AI-native workflow coordinates hardware and software changes in a single loop guided by physical tool feedback. The Lighthouse project grounds that vision in a demanding system target: delivering an XR compute subsystem within a 3\ W wearable envelope. The 2030 engineering milestone asks whether an AI-native design system can carry that compact prompt all the way to a verified design that passes physical signoff, while a separate methodological test asks whether the workflow delivers better architectural trade-offs, lower total engineering cost for a comparable result, or both against a credible matched baseline.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Match the workflow layer to the problem.** Use point assistance (Layer 1) for individual tasks, container-bound optimization (Layer 2) for search within prescribed templates, and an AI-native design system (Layer 3) when the study calls for coordinated hardware–software revisions beyond those templates.
- **Decouple operational layers from method families.** Prediction, generation, and optimization operate across all three layers, so generating code does not by itself establish an AI-native design capability.
- **Maintain rigorous experimental provenance.** Preserve versioned artifacts, input traces, tool settings, and random seeds to make every architectural finding reproducible and auditable.
- **Audit design quality and engineering effort jointly.** Benchmark automated systems against matched human baselines with identical budgets. True efficiency requires improving silicon PPA, reducing total design effort, or both.
- **Preserve human authority over irreversible commitments.** Automation accelerates exploration and surfaces Pareto trade-offs, but human architects define the requirements, examine the evidence, and authorize silicon tapeout.
:::

@sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales examines the transistor scaling limits, workload shifts, and verification bottlenecks that make this transition necessary.
